title: Exact kNN and why it doesn't scale
summary: Brute force search has an arithmetic intensity of 0.5 FLOPs per byte against a machine balance of 4, so it is memory bound by eight times and behaves like a table scan. Measured: 93 ms and 10.8 queries per second at a million vectors, exactly as the roofline predicts.
html:
Phase 2 is twenty one days on one question: how do you find the nearest vectors without looking at all of them? Today is about why you have to ask, and the answer is not the one the FLOP count suggests.

Your Day 8 search already does exact k-nearest-neighbour search. Score every vector, sort, take the top k. It is correct by construction: no approximation, no tuning, guaranteed right answer. It is also the thing that breaks first.

The obvious accounting, which is wrong

One query against a million 1024-dimension vectors. Each dot product is 1024 multiplies and 1024 adds, so:

FLOPs per query = 2 x 1024 x 1,000,000 = 2.048 GFLOP

A server CPU does a couple of hundred GFLOP/s. Two GFLOP should take about ten milliseconds. Fine.

It does not take ten milliseconds, and the reason is the number nobody quotes.

Arithmetic intensity

Count the bytes as well as the operations. The query vector is 4 KB and stays in cache. Every document vector is read once from memory and never reused:

bytes read per query = 1,000,000 x 1024 x 4 = 4.096 GB
FLOPs per query      = 2.048 GFLOP

arithmetic intensity = 2.048 / 4.096 = 0.5 FLOPs per byte

Half a floating point operation per byte fetched. Now compare that against machine balance, peak FLOPs divided by memory bandwidth, which is how many FLOPs a machine must do per byte to keep its arithmetic units busy:

MachinePeakBandwidthBalanceWe have 0.5
server CPU200 GFLOP/s50 GB/s4.0memory bound by 8x
fast CPU400 GFLOP/s100 GB/s4.0memory bound by 8x
GPU (HBM)30 TFLOP/s2 TB/s15.0memory bound by 30x

Exact kNN is not a compute problem. It is a streaming problem that happens to do a little arithmetic on the way past. The CPU spends most of its time waiting for memory, and buying a faster CPU changes nothing.

You have seen this shape before. It is a table scan. No index, no locality to exploit, no way to skip anything, throughput set by how fast you can move bytes off the medium.

So the floor is bandwidth

at   25 GB/s:  163.84 ms/query  ->     6.1 queries/sec
at   50 GB/s:   81.92 ms/query  ->    12.2 queries/sec
at  100 GB/s:   40.96 ms/query  ->    24.4 queries/sec
at 2000 GB/s:    2.05 ms/query  ->   488.3 queries/sec  (GPU, vectors in VRAM)

Those are floors, assuming perfect streaming and zero overhead. I ran the real thing with numpy on this machine:

   N vectors      GB   ms/query   GB/s eff       q/s
      10,000    0.04       0.69       59.7    1457.5
     100,000    0.41      10.44       39.2      95.8
     500,000    2.05      59.40       34.5      16.8
   1,000,000    4.10      92.97       44.1      10.8

93 ms and 10.8 queries per second at a million vectors, against a predicted 82 ms. The effective bandwidth sits between 35 and 60 GB/s, which is what a memory bound kernel looks like. The model was right, which means you can now predict this for any corpus size without measuring.

Batching changes the arithmetic, not the latency

If several queries arrive together, read each document vector once and score it against all of them. The bytes stay the same and the FLOPs multiply:

batch    1: intensity   0.5 FLOPs/byte   memory bound
batch    4: intensity   2.0              memory bound
batch    8: intensity   4.0              at the balance point
batch   32: intensity  16.0              compute bound
batch  128: intensity  64.0              compute bound

Eight queries is enough to flip a typical CPU from memory bound to compute bound. This is why GPU brute force search is viable for offline or batch workloads, and it is the same trick as turning random reads into one sequential scan.

It does nothing for a user waiting on one question. A single query still has to touch every byte, and no batching rescues p99 latency for interactive search.

The actual wall

     10,000 vectors:    0.04 GB      0.82 ms/query
  1,000,000 vectors:    4.10 GB     81.92 ms/query
100,000,000 vectors:  409.60 GB   8192.00 ms/query

Linear, forever. Every optimisation available here is a constant factor: SIMD, threads, float16, a GPU. Useful, and none of them touch the exponent. A hundred million vectors is eight seconds per query on a CPU and will not fit in VRAM at all.

Phase 2 is about getting off the linear curve, and every technique in it is a way of not looking at most of your data.

Two things that look like fixes

The sort. Day 8 sorted all N scores to take the top k, which is O(N log N) on top of the scan. Use a partial selection instead: np.argpartition is linear and only guarantees the top k are in the first k slots, unordered, which is all you need before a final sort of k elements. Real improvement, and it does not change anything above, because you were memory bound before you reached the sort.

Sharding. Split the corpus across M machines, search each in parallel, merge the M top-k lists. Latency drops by a factor of M, and for a distributed systems person this is the obvious move.

It is also a constant factor wearing a costume. Each shard is still doing a linear scan of N/M vectors, you have added fan-out and a merge step to the critical path, and your p99 is now the slowest shard rather than the average one. Ten times the hardware buys ten times the corpus at the same latency. The curve is unchanged, you have just moved along it at considerable expense. An index changes the curve, which is why it is worth twenty days.

When exact search is the right answer

Two cases, and both matter.

Small corpora. At 10,000 vectors brute force ran in 0.69 ms and served 1,457 queries per second, because 40 MB fits in cache and streams beautifully. An approximate index at that size adds build time, memory, tuning parameters and a recall loss, to fix a problem you do not have. FAISS's own guidance is to use a flat index below roughly this scale. If your corpus is a product manual, stop reading Phase 2 and ship the loop.

As ground truth. This is the one people forget. Recall@k for an approximate index is defined against the exact answer. You cannot measure how much recall your HNSW graph loses without a brute force reference to compare it to. Every tuning curve in the next twenty days is plotted against exact search, which means you will keep running it long after you stop serving with it.

You now know the cost of being exactly right. Tomorrow makes the tradeoff explicit: recall, latency and memory, and why you only ever get to pick two.
exercise:
1. Measure your own bandwidth floor. Generate a random float32 matrix of 200,000 by 768, normalize the rows, and time X @ q for a single query. Divide the matrix size in bytes by the time. That number is your machine's effective memory bandwidth on this kernel, and it sets the floor for every exact search you will ever run on it.

2. Find your own crossover. Repeat at 10k, 50k, 200k and 1M rows and note where per-query latency crosses whatever your product's budget is, 10 ms or 50 ms or whatever you actually have. That row is the corpus size at which you are forced to care about Phase 2. Below it, brute force is correct and simpler.

3. Watch batching flip the bottleneck. At 200k rows, time a single query, then a batch of 32 queries. Divide the batch time by 32. Per-query cost should drop several fold even though the total work went up. That is arithmetic intensity moving, and you just measured the effect the table above predicts.
